pages.title: Unit 4A: Sequences and Infinite Series
pages.body_latex:
\chapter*{Unit 4A: Sequences and Infinite Series}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Unit 4A: Sequences and Infinite Series}


A finite sum ends because the list of terms ends. An infinite series does not. That small change forces a new kind of question: not merely how to add, but whether the partial sums settle toward a finite number at all. The subject therefore begins with sequences, because a series converges precisely when its sequence of partial sums converges.

The unit develops a disciplined collection of tests rather than a bag of incantations. Geometric and telescoping series can often be summed exactly. Positive-term series can be studied by comparison or integration. Alternating signs can create convergence through cancellation. Ratio and root tests expose exponential behavior. The final goal is not memorizing names; it is learning to recognize structure and choose an efficient argument.

\begin{bgconcept}[title={The central distinction}]
A sequence is an ordered list \(\{a_n\}\). A series is the sequence of partial sums generated by adding its terms:
\[
s_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_n.
\]
The series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) converges to \(S\) when \(s_N\to S\).
\end{bgconcept}

\section*{Unit map}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Sequences, recursive descriptions, and limits
\item Monotone and bounded sequences
\item Infinite series and partial sums
\item Geometric, telescoping, harmonic, and \(p\)-series
\item Integral, comparison, alternating, ratio, and root tests
\item Absolute and conditional convergence
\item Test-selection strategy, reviews, and two practice exams
\end{enumerate}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={A first glimpse of analysis}]
Convergence is a promise about every sufficiently late term or partial sum, not a report about the first hundred values displayed by a calculator. Later analysis courses make that promise precise through quantified definitions and Cauchy criteria. This unit keeps the proofs accessible while preserving the logical distinction between numerical evidence and mathematical guarantee.
\end{bgadvanced}

pages.body_latex:
\section{Limit Laws for Sequences}

\lessonobjective{use algebraic limit laws to combine convergent sequences and identify indeterminate forms that require more work.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Algebra works after convergence is established}]

If two sequences converge, their sums, differences, products, and appropriate quotients behave as expected. These laws let us replace complicated expressions by limits of simpler pieces. The laws do not say that every expression with infinity symbols can be manipulated like arithmetic. ``Infinity over infinity'' is not a number; it is a warning that dominant growth must be compared.



A reliable strategy is to normalize by the largest power, factor a dominant term, rationalize a radical, or use a known function limit. Before applying a quotient law, verify that the denominator limit is nonzero. Before moving a continuous function through a limit, check that the function is continuous at the limiting value and that the sequence stays in its domain.

\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={Why algebra survives the limiting process}]
If two sequences settle near \(A\) and \(B\), then their late sums, products, and valid quotients should settle near the corresponding algebraic combinations. The limit laws formalize this stability and reduce complicated sequences to simpler components.

The laws are not permission to substitute blindly. Division requires a nonzero limiting denominator, and roots require valid domains. Identify component limits, verify the operation is defined at those limits, and only then combine them.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={The sum law is an error estimate}]
If \(a_n\to A\) and \(b_n\to B\), then
\[
|(a_n+b_n)-(A+B)|\le |a_n-A|+|b_n-B|.
\]
Making each component error less than \(\varepsilon/2\) makes the total error less than \(\varepsilon\).
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Limit-law summary}]

If \(a_n\to A\) and \(b_n\to B\), then
\[
a_n\pm b_n\to A\pm B,\quad a_nb_n\to AB,
\]
and \(a_n/b_n\to A/B\) when \(B\ne0\). Continuous functions preserve limits where defined.

\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={A radical sequence}]

Evaluate \(a_n=\sqrt{n^2+4n}-n\). Rationalize:
\[
a_n=\frac{4n}{\sqrt{n^2+4n}+n}
=\frac{4}{\sqrt{1+4/n}+1}\to2.
\]
The original form \(\infty-\infty\) concealed a finite difference.

\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A quotient needs a domain check}]
Evaluate
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n^2-5n}{n^2+3}.
\]
Divide by \(n^2\):
\[
\frac{2-5/n}{1+3/n^2}.
\]
The numerator tends to \(2\) and the denominator to \(1\). Since the limiting denominator is nonzero, the quotient law applies and the limit is \(2\).
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={The quotient law does not evaluate zero over zero}]
When numerator and denominator both approach zero, the quotient law is inconclusive. Rewrite or compare rates instead.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u4a-sequence_limit_laws-01}{expression}{3}[Quick check]

Evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3n^2-1}{n^2+5}\).

\begin{bghint}

Divide by \(n^2\).

\end{bghint}

\begin{bgreveal}

\[\frac{3-1/n^2}{1+5/n^2}\to3.\]

\end{bgreveal}

\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}

\item Evaluate \((n^2+1)^{1/2}/n\).

\item Find \(\lim (2+1/n)^3\).

\item Explain why the quotient law cannot be applied to \(n/(1/n)\) using a denominator limit of zero.

\item Rationalize \(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n\).

\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: The Squeeze Theorem for Sequences
pages.body_latex:
\section{The Squeeze Theorem for Sequences}

\lessonobjective{use upper and lower bounds to prove convergence when direct algebra does not reveal the limit.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Control can matter more than an exact formula}]

Some sequences contain oscillatory factors that never converge by themselves. If that oscillation is multiplied by a magnitude shrinking to zero, exact values become irrelevant. Bounding the sequence between two simpler sequences can force a limit even when the internal behavior remains complicated.



The sequence version of the Squeeze Theorem works exactly like its function counterpart. The important work is choosing bounds that hold for every sufficiently large integer. Absolute-value inequalities are especially efficient: proving \(|a_n-L|\le b_n\) with \(b_n\to0\) proves \(a_n\to L\). This form also previews the error estimates used later for alternating and Taylor series.

\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={Control can replace direct computation}]
An oscillating sequence may be difficult to simplify directly. The Squeeze Theorem ignores the exact internal motion and traps the sequence between two simpler sequences. If both walls close onto the same limit, the middle sequence has nowhere else to go.

The method is especially useful when a bounded factor is multiplied by something that shrinks to zero. The proof concerns the shrinking envelope, not the oscillation inside it.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={Both boundaries eventually enter the same band}]
Once the lower and upper sequences lie inside an \(\varepsilon\)-band around \(L\), every trapped middle term lies inside as well. The formal proof simply chooses a cutoff large enough for both boundaries.
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Sequence squeeze theorem}]

If \(b_n\le a_n\le c_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), and \(b_n\to L\) and \(c_n\to L\), then \(a_n\to L\).

\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={An oscillating numerator}]

Since \(-1\le\cos n\le1\),
\[
-\frac1n\le\frac{\cos n}{n}\le\frac1n.
\]
Both bounds approach zero, so
\[
\frac{\cos n}{n}\to0.
\]

\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Bound the absolute value first}]
For \(a_n=\cos(n^2)/\sqrt n\), the numerator need not converge, but
\[
|a_n|\le\frac1{\sqrt n}\to0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
-\frac1{\sqrt n}\le a_n\le\frac1{\sqrt n}.
\]
Both bounds approach zero, so \(a_n\to0\).
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={The trap must actually close}]
The bounds \(-1\le a_n\le1\) do not imply convergence. The sequence \((-1)^n\) satisfies them and still oscillates.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u4a-squeeze_theorem_for_sequences-01}{expression}{0}[Quick check]

Evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sin n}{n}\).

\begin{bghint}

Use \(|\sin n|\le1\).

\end{bghint}

\begin{bgreveal}

\[\left|\frac{\sin n}{n}\right|\le\frac1n\to0,\quad\text{so the limit is }0.\]

\end{bgreveal}

\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}

\item Prove \((-1)^n/n^2\to0\).

\item Show \(\sqrt[n]{n}\to1\) using logarithms or known bounds.

\item Give an example where two bounds approach different limits and therefore do not determine the middle limit.

\item Explain the phrase ``for all sufficiently large \(n\).

\end{bgexercises}

pages.body_latex:
\section{Integral-Test Remainder Estimates}

\lessonobjective{bound the tail of a convergent positive series and determine how many terms guarantee a target accuracy.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Convergence without an error estimate is often not enough}]

Knowing that a series converges answers an existence question, but applications require a numerical guarantee. For a positive decreasing series, the tail after \(N\) terms can be trapped between two improper integrals. These bounds convert a convergence proof into a practical stopping rule.



The remainder \(R_N=S-s_N\) is positive for positive-term series. The lower and upper integral bounds differ only by shifting the starting point, and both become small as \(N\) grows. To guarantee accuracy, solve the upper-bound inequality rather than calculating many partial sums and hoping their decimals have stabilized.

\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={Convergence is only the first question}]
Once a positive decreasing series is known to converge, practical work asks how much remains after the first \(N\) terms. The same rectangles used in the Integral Test trap the remainder \(R_N=S-s_N\) between two improper integrals.

The estimate is useful because it turns an inaccessible infinite tail into an explicit inequality. To guarantee a requested accuracy, solve the upper-bound inequality for \(N\), then round upward. The bound is a certificate: it may not equal the true error, but it proves the error cannot exceed the stated amount.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={The omitted rectangles are trapped by adjacent areas}]
For decreasing \(f\), each omitted rectangle lies below the area beginning one unit earlier and above the area beginning at its own right endpoint. Summing those comparisons yields
\[
\int_{N+1}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx\le R_N\le\int_N^{\infty}f(x)\,dx.
\]
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Remainder bounds}]

If the Integral Test hypotheses hold, then
\[
\int_{N+1}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx\le R_N\le\int_N^{\infty}f(x)\,dx.
\]

\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={How many terms for a cubic p-series?}]

For \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^3\),
\[
R_N\le\int_N^{\infty}x^{-3}\,dx=\frac1{2N^2}.
\]
To guarantee \(R_N<0.001\), require \(1/(2N^2)<0.001\), so \(N>\sqrt{500}\). Thus \(N=23\) suffices.

\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Choose N from a target error}]
How many terms of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^4\) guarantee error below \(10^{-4}\)? For \(f(x)=x^{-4}\),
\[
R_N\le\int_N^\infty x^{-4}\,dx=\frac{1}{3N^3}.
\]
Require
\[
\frac{1}{3N^3}<10^{-4},
\qquad N^3>\frac{10^4}{3}.
\]
Since \(15^3=3375>3333.\overline3\), taking \(N=15\) guarantees the desired accuracy.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={Use the correct endpoint for the upper bound}]
For a decreasing positive series, \(\int_{N+1}^{\infty}f\le R_N\le\int_N^{\infty}f\). Swapping the endpoints can turn a claimed guarantee into a guess.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u4a-integral_test_remainder_estimates-01}{expression}{1/(2*N^2)}[Quick check]

Give an upper bound for the remainder of \(\sum1/n^3\) after \(N\) terms.

\begin{bghint}

Integrate \(x^{-3}\) from \(N\) to infinity.

\end{bghint}

\begin{bgreveal}

\[R_N\le\int_N^{\infty}x^{-3}\,dx=\frac1{2N^2}.\]

\end{bgreveal}

\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}

\item Find a remainder bound for \(\sum1/n^2\).

\item How many terms ensure error below \(10^{-4}\) for \(\sum1/n^2\)?

\item Explain why the bound may be larger than the actual error.

\item Use both lower and upper bounds to bracket the total sum from a partial sum.

\end{bgexercises}

The Limit Comparison Test
pages.body_latex:
\section{The Limit Comparison Test}

\lessonobjective{use asymptotic ratios to compare positive series when direct inequalities are awkward.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Asymptotic sameness is often enough}]

Two positive sequences can differ in lower-order details while having the same long-run scale. If their ratio approaches a finite positive constant, then neither is eventually dramatically larger than the other. Their series therefore share the same convergence behavior.



Limit comparison is particularly efficient for rational functions of \(n\), radicals, and expressions whose dominant terms are obvious. It classifies convergence but usually does not produce the sum. The comparison sequence should be simple and known, most often a \(p\)-series or geometric series. A ratio limit of zero or infinity may still provide information, but the standard equivalence conclusion requires a positive finite constant.

\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgdecision}[title={Choose the benchmark before taking the limit}]
Ignore lower-order terms and identify the dominant power, logarithm, or exponential behavior. Select \(b_n\) from a familiar family with that scale. Then compute \(\lim a_n/b_n\); a positive finite limit means the two series share a convergence type.
\end{bgdecision}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={Asymptotic proportionality replaces a hard inequality}]
Exact term-by-term inequalities can be awkward when formulas contain several competing pieces. If \(a_n/b_n\to L\) with \(0<L<\infty\), then the terms are eventually comparable by positive constant multiples. Neither series can have a fundamentally different convergence behavior from the other.

The benchmark should match the dominant size of the target term. For rational powers, compare leading powers of \(n\); for radicals, factor the highest power inside the root. The limit must be positive and finite. A limit of zero or infinity may still suggest a one-sided comparison, but it is not the standard Limit Comparison Test conclusion.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={A limit near L produces two ordinary comparisons}]
Choose, for example, \(\varepsilon=L/2\). Eventually
\[
\frac L2<\frac{a_n}{b_n}<\frac{3L}{2},
\]
so \((L/2)b_n<a_n<(3L/2)b_n\). Direct comparison then transfers convergence or divergence.
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Limit Comparison Test}]

For positive \(a_n,b_n\), if
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}=c
\quad\text{with }0<c<\infty,
\]
then \(\sum a_n\) and \(\sum b_n\) either both converge or both diverge.

\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Dominant powers}]

Let
\[
a_n=\frac{3n+1}{n^3-4},\qquad b_n=\frac1{n^2}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{a_n}{b_n}=\frac{n^2(3n+1)}{n^3-4}\to3.
\]
Since \(\sum1/n^2\) converges, so does \(\sum a_n\).

\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Leading powers select the benchmark}]
Test
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{4n^2+1}{n^4+7}.
\]
The dominant behavior is \(4n^2/n^4=4/n^2\), so use \(b_n=1/n^2\). Then
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^2(4n^2+1)}{n^4+7}=4.
\]
Because \(4\) is positive and finite and \(\sum1/n^2\) converges, the given series converges.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={State the benchmark series, not only the ratio}]
A correct solution identifies \(b_n\), evaluates the ratio limit, states that the limit is positive and finite, and classifies \(\sum b_n\).
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u4a-limit_comparison_test-01}{expression}{3}[Quick check]

For \(a_n=(3n+1)/(n^3-4)\) and \(b_n=1/n^2\), find \(\lim a_n/b_n\).

\begin{bghint}

Multiply \(a_n\) by \(n^2\) and compare highest powers.

\end{bghint}

\begin{bgreveal}

The ratio approaches \(3\).

\end{bgreveal}

\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}

\item Classify \(\sum(n+2)/(n^2+1)\).

\item Compare \(1/\sqrt{n^2+n}\) with \(1/n\).

\item Explain why a ratio limit of \(1\) is called asymptotic equivalence.

\item Give an example where direct comparison is easier than limit comparison.

\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Alternating Series
Alternating-Series Error Estimates
pages.body_latex:
\section{Alternating-Series Error Estimates}

\lessonobjective{use the first omitted term to control approximation error for a convergent alternating series.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={The next term measures the remaining uncertainty}]

For a decreasing alternating series, successive partial sums lie on opposite sides of the limit. The true sum is trapped between two consecutive partial sums, so the distance from either one to the limit cannot exceed the next term magnitude. This unusually clean estimate makes alternating series computationally attractive.



The bound is a guarantee, not an exact error. To meet a tolerance, solve \(b_{N+1}<\varepsilon\). Then check indexing carefully: the first omitted term after \(s_N\) is term \(N+1\). If the series begins at another index, translate the term count rather than mechanically substituting \(N+1\).

\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={The next term controls the entire remaining error}]
For an alternating series satisfying the test, the true sum lies between every pair of consecutive partial sums. The error after \(N\) terms is therefore no larger than the distance to the next endpoint of that bracket, namely \(b_{N+1}\).

This unusually simple bound turns convergence into a practical approximation method. To guarantee a tolerance, solve \(b_{N+1}<\varepsilon\). The sign of the first omitted term also tells which side of the true sum the approximation lies on.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={The true sum stays inside the next bracket}]
The alternating partial sums nest around \(S\). Since \(S\) lies between \(s_N\) and \(s_{N+1}\), its distance from \(s_N\) is at most \(|s_{N+1}-s_N|=b_{N+1}\).
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Alternating remainder estimate}]

Under the Alternating Series Test hypotheses,
\[
|S-s_N|\le b_{N+1}.
\]

\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Approximate \(\ln2\)}]

Using
\[
\ln2=1-\frac12+\frac13-\cdots,
\]
we want error below \(0.01\). Since the next term after \(N\) terms has magnitude \(1/(N+1)\), require \(1/(N+1)<0.01\), so \(N\ge100\) guarantees the tolerance.

\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Guarantee four-decimal accuracy}]
For
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^3},
\]
how many terms guarantee error below \(10^{-4}\)? The alternating remainder satisfies
\[
|R_N|\le \frac{1}{(N+1)^3}.
\]
Require \((N+1)^3>10^4\). Since \(22^3=10648\), \(N+1=22\) works, so \(N=21\) terms guarantee the requested accuracy.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={Use the first omitted term}]
After summing through \(n=N\), the bound is \(b_{N+1}\), not \(b_N\). This one-index error can invalidate an accuracy claim.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u4a-alternating_series_error-01}{expression}{1/(N+1)}[Quick check]

What bounds the error after \(N\) terms of the alternating harmonic series?

\begin{bghint}

Use the magnitude of the first omitted term.

\end{bghint}

\begin{bgreveal}

\[|S-s_N|\le\frac1{N+1}.\]

\end{bgreveal}

\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}

\item How many terms guarantee error below \(10^{-3}\)?

\item Approximate \(\sum(-1)^{n-1}/n^2\) with four terms and state an error bound.

\item Explain why the true sum lies between consecutive partial sums.

\item Compare this error estimate with the integral remainder estimate.

\end{bgexercises}

The Ratio Test
The Root Test
pages.body_latex:
\section{The Root Test}

\lessonobjective{use nth roots to detect terms raised to the nth power and compare the Root Test with the Ratio Test.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={nth powers reveal themselves under nth roots}]

When an entire expression is raised to the \(n\)th power, taking an \(n\)th root removes that outer exponent and exposes the effective geometric ratio. The Root Test is therefore natural for terms such as \(((2n+1)/(3n+2))^n\) and less natural for plain rational functions.



The conclusion mirrors the Ratio Test. A limit below one gives absolute convergence; above one gives divergence; equal to one is inconclusive. In more advanced analysis, the test is often stated with a limit superior because the ordinary limit need not exist. Calculus examples are usually designed so the simpler limit exists.

\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={Extract the effective exponential base}]
The Root Test asks for the long-run base hidden inside \(|a_n|\) by examining \(\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\). It is especially effective when the entire term is raised to the \(n\)th power or contains several exponential factors.

Its conclusions parallel the Ratio Test: a limit below one gives absolute convergence, a limit above one gives divergence, and a limit equal to one is inconclusive. Simplify the \(n\)th root before taking the limit; that is where the method earns its keep.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={The extracted base controls the whole term}]
If the root limit is below one, choose \(r<1\) above the limit. Eventually \(\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}<r\), hence \(|a_n|<r^n\), and geometric comparison proves absolute convergence.
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Root Test}]

Let
\[
L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}.
\]
If \(L<1\), the series converges absolutely. If \(L>1\), it diverges. If \(L=1\), the test is inconclusive.

\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={An nth-power series}]

For
\[
a_n=\left(\frac{2n+1}{3n+2}\right)^n,
\]
we have
\[
\sqrt[n]{a_n}=\frac{2n+1}{3n+2}\to\frac23<1.
\]
Therefore the series converges.

\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={An nth power reveals its own base}]
Test
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2n+1}{3n+4}\right)^n.
\]
Then
\[
\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}=\frac{2n+1}{3n+4}\to\frac23.
\]
Since \(2/3<1\), the series converges absolutely by the Root Test.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={Take the root of the whole magnitude}]
The test uses \(\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\). Applying the root to only one factor can destroy the expression’s effective base.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u4a-root_test-01}{expression}{2/3}[Quick check]

Find the Root-Test limit for \(a_n=((2n+1)/(3n+2))^n\).

\begin{bghint}

The nth root cancels the outer power.

\end{bghint}

\begin{bgreveal}

\[\sqrt[n]{a_n}=\frac{2n+1}{3n+2}\to\frac23.\]

\end{bgreveal}

\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}

\item Apply the Root Test to \(\sum[(n+1)/(2n)]^n\).

\item Explain why it is inconclusive for \(\sum1/n^3\).

\item Compare the algebra required by root and ratio tests for \((n/(n+1))^{n^2}\).

\item State the limit-superior version informally.

\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Choosing a Convergence Test
Why Convergence Is About Tails: A Cauchy Preview
pages.body_latex:
\section{Why Convergence Is About Tails: A Cauchy Preview}

\lessonobjective{explain convergence in terms of tails becoming small and connect this idea to later analysis.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={A convergent series eventually has negligible tails}]

If partial sums approach a number \(S\), then two sufficiently late partial sums must be close to each other. Their difference is a finite tail \(a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_n\). Thus convergence can be described without knowing \(S\): every sufficiently late tail must be small. This is the Cauchy viewpoint.



For positive series, tail smallness means little mass remains. For alternating series, cancellation can make tails small even when absolute magnitudes have infinite total. The Cauchy criterion explains why convergence tests work: each one provides a different method for controlling every possible late tail, not merely a few computed partial sums.

\end{bgexposition}

\begin{bgtranslation}[title={The Cauchy criterion controls whole tails}]
The condition is not merely \(|s_{n+1}-s_n|\to0\), which says only that individual terms vanish. It requires every finite tail \(a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_n\) to be small once both endpoints are sufficiently late. The harmonic series shows why the stronger statement is necessary.
\end{bgtranslation}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={Convergence can be recognized without knowing the limit}]
The usual definition says partial sums approach some number \(S\), but the Cauchy viewpoint asks whether late partial sums become close to one another. For a series, this means every sufficiently late finite block \(a_{n+1}+\cdots+a_m\) must be small.

This tail criterion unifies the convergence tests: each successful test ultimately proves that distant tails can be controlled. The deeper theorem that every Cauchy sequence of real numbers actually converges relies on the completeness of \(\mathbb R\), one of the central structural ideas of real analysis.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgdefinition}[title={Cauchy criterion for a series}]
A series \(\sum a_n\) converges exactly when, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(N\) such that whenever \(m>n\ge N\),
\[
|a_{n+1}+\cdots+a_m|<\varepsilon.
\]
\end{bgdefinition}
\begin{bgproofidea}[title={Why this points toward real analysis}]
Convergence immediately implies the Cauchy property by the triangle inequality. The converse uses completeness: the real numbers contain the limit of every Cauchy sequence. That structural fact is deeper than any one convergence test.
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Cauchy criterion for series}]

A series \(\sum a_n\) converges exactly when, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(N\) such that
\[
\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n}a_k\right|<\varepsilon
\]
whenever \(n\ge m\ge N\).

\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={A geometric tail}]

For \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n\) with \(|r|<1\), a tail beginning at \(m\) has magnitude at most
\[
\frac{|r|^m}{1-|r|},
\]
which approaches zero as \(m\to\infty\). The estimate proves tail control directly.

\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A geometric tail is uniformly small}]
For \(|r|<1\), consider \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n\). If \(m>n\), then
\[
\left|\sum_{k=n+1}^{m}r^k\right|
\le \sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty}|r|^k
=\frac{|r|^{n+1}}{1-|r|}.
\]
The right side approaches zero as \(n\to\infty\), independently of how far \(m\) lies beyond \(n\). Thus all sufficiently late partial sums are close to one another.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={Pairwise closeness must hold for every later endpoint}]
It is not enough that consecutive partial sums become close. The harmonic increments \(1/n\) approach zero, yet sufficiently long blocks can still have substantial size.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{u4a-cauchy_criterion_preview-01}{expression}{r^m/(1-r)}[Quick check]

For \(0<r<1\), give the infinite geometric tail beginning with \(r^m\).

\begin{bghint}

Use the first-term-over-one-minus-ratio formula.

\end{bghint}

\begin{bgreveal}

\[r^m+r^{m+1}+\cdots=\frac{r^m}{1-r}.\]

\end{bgreveal}

\end{bgcheck}

\begin{bgexercises}

\item Explain why the nth-term test follows from the Cauchy criterion.

\item Show that a harmonic tail from \(m\) to \(2m\) is bounded below away from zero.

\item Describe how absolute convergence controls tails.

\item Why does this criterion depend on completeness of the real numbers?

\end{bgexercises}

\section*{Unit 4A Reference Sheet}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\textbf{Geometric:} \(\sum ar^n=a/(1-r)\) for \(|r|<1\).

\textbf{\(p\)-series:} \(\sum1/n^p\) converges iff \(p>1\).

\textbf{nth term:} nonzero term limit implies divergence.

\textbf{Integral Test:} positive, continuous, decreasing interpolation.

\textbf{Comparison:} smaller than convergent; larger than divergent.

\textbf{Alternating:} decreasing magnitudes to zero.

\textbf{Ratio/Root:} limit below one converges absolutely; above one diverges; equal one inconclusive.

\textbf{Alternating error:} at most first omitted magnitude.
\end{multicols}
